subject: Mixed
description: Hard-difficulty practice set (20 questions) covering: Kinesio Therapeutics, Medicine, OBGY, Pathology & Microbiology, Pharmacology, Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills, Physiology, Physiotherapy in Community Health, Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition, Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition, Physiotherapy in Neurosciences, Psychiatry, Psychology.

questions.question: Platelets are formed by pinching off bits of cytoplasm from which giant, multinucleated bone marrow cell?

options.A: The granular megakaryocyte
options.B: The erythroblast
options.D: The lymphoblast

questions.explanation: Platelets are formed within the cytoplasm of the granular megakaryocyte by pinching off bits of cytoplasm, released into circulation when the cell dies — a single megakaryocyte can produce 2,000-4,000 platelets by this process.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: Platelets or Thrombocytes — Thrombopoiesis
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: A Type I (anaphylactic) drug allergy reaction is mediated by which antibody, fixed to mast cells?

options.A: IgE
options.B: IgG only
options.D: No antibody is involved — it is purely T-cell mediated

questions.explanation: Type I (anaphylactic) reactions are mediated by IgE (reaginic) antibodies fixed to mast cells; on re-exposure to the drug, the antigen-antibody reaction on the mast cell surface releases histamine and other mediators, producing urticaria, bronchospasm, or anaphylactic shock — a rapid-onset 'immediate hypersensitivity' reaction.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Adverse Drug Effects — Drug Allergy, Mechanisms
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Carcinosarcoma is an example of a mixed tumour because it combines:

options.A: Two different carcinomas of the same epithelial origin
options.B: A malignant tumour of epithelium (carcinoma) with a malignant tumour of mesenchymal tissue (sarcoma) in the same lesion
options.C: A benign and a malignant tumour of the same tissue type
options.D: Tissue from all three germ cell layers

questions.explanation: Carcinosarcoma is the rare combination of a malignant epithelial tumour (carcinoma) and a malignant mesenchymal tumour (sarcoma) occurring together in the same lesion, such as in the thyroid.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours
questions.subject: Pathology & Microbiology

questions.question: Which of the following is cited as a genuine limitation of mortality data, particularly relevant to developing countries like India?

options.A: Incomplete reporting of deaths and lack of accuracy in recording age/cause of death
options.B: Mortality data is always 100% complete and accurate worldwide
options.C: Death certificates do not exist in any country
options.D: Mortality data cannot be tabulated by any coding system

questions.explanation: Incomplete reporting of deaths is not usually a problem in developed countries, but can be considerable in India and other developing countries. Combined with inaccuracies in age/cause recording (often due to lack of diagnostic evidence, inexperienced certifying doctors, or absence of postmortem examination), this is a genuine limitation of mortality data quality.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised physical complication of a severe, chronic cough?

options.A: Cough fractures (fractured ribs) and hernias
options.B: Permanent hearing loss
options.D: Osteoarthritis of the knee

questions.explanation: Chronic, forceful coughing can cause 'cough fractures' of the ribs and hernias, due to the repeated high intra-thoracic and intra-abdominal pressures generated. Stress urinary incontinence is another common, often under-reported complication, especially in women.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Cough
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: In the two-state receptor model (Ra = active, Ri = inactive conformation), an inverse agonist is one that:

options.A: Binds Ra and Ri with exactly equal affinity, producing no net change
options.B: Has high affinity for the Ri (inactive) state, shifting equilibrium away from Ra and producing an effect opposite to the agonist
options.C: Cannot bind the receptor at all in either state
options.D: Only functions on receptors with no baseline (constitutive) activity

questions.explanation: An inverse agonist preferentially binds and stabilizes the inactive (Ri) receptor conformation. This only produces an observable opposite effect on receptors that show constitutive activation (some baseline Ra signal even without agonist) — by pulling the equilibrium further toward Ri, it reduces signalling below the unstimulated baseline.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: In the first week postpartum, there is a secondary increase in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelets. What clinical risk does this hypercoagulable state primarily raise?

options.A: Risk of thrombosis
options.B: Risk of spontaneous bleeding
options.D: No clinical significance

questions.explanation: The secondary rise in fibrinogen, factor VIII, and platelet count (with increased platelet adhesiveness) during the first postpartum week increases the risk of thrombosis — one reason early ambulation and postpartum exercise are actively encouraged, since enhanced fibrinolytic activity in the first few days acts as a partial protective counter-mechanism.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Blood Values
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: In an ERECT chest radiograph, the first and most important radiographic sign of elevated left ventricular pressure (early left ventricular failure) is:

options.A: Upper lobe blood diversion (shunting of blood to the upper zones)
options.B: A completely normal-appearing chest X-ray in all cases
options.C: Immediate cavitation of the lung fields
options.D: Loss of the diaphragm outline

questions.explanation: As left atrial pressure rises, blood is shunted to the upper zones — upper lobe blood diversion — which is the first and most important radiographic sign of elevated left ventricular pressure on an erect film. This sign cannot be reliably assessed on a supine radiograph due to redistribution of blood flow in that position.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Cardiac Failure
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Chronic pain syndrome, as distinguished from ordinary chronic inflammation, is defined as a state that:

options.A: Persists longer than 6 months, with pain that cannot be linked to an identifiable source of irritation or inflammation, and includes physical, emotional, and psychosocial functional limitations
options.B: Always resolves completely within 48 hours
options.C: Is defined purely by the presence of visible swelling
options.D: Only ever occurs immediately after acute injury, never later

questions.explanation: Chronic pain syndrome persists longer than 6 months, includes pain that cannot be linked to an identifiable source of ongoing irritation or inflammation, and encompasses functional limitations and disability across physical, emotional, and psychosocial dimensions — distinct from simple chronic inflammation from ongoing tissue irritation.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 10: Soft Tissue Injury, Repair, and Management — Chronic Pain Syndrome
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics

questions.question: Peripheral oedema in a respiratory patient most commonly suggests which underlying process?

options.A: Right heart failure, potentially due to cor pulmonale (right ventricular failure secondary to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction)
options.B: Left ventricular failure exclusively
options.C: Normal ageing with no pathological significance
options.D: Acute asthma exacerbation

questions.explanation: Peripheral oedema in a respiratory patient suggests right heart failure, which may result from cor pulmonale — right ventricular failure secondary to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction from underlying chronic lung disease. It can also occur from salt/water retention with high-dose corticosteroid use.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Other Symptoms
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: On a chest radiograph, emphysema characteristically produces overinflation of the lungs, flattening of the diaphragm, and:

options.A: An enlarged, apparently big heart with an increased cardiothoracic ratio
options.B: An apparently SMALL heart with a DECREASED cardiothoracic ratio, due to diaphragmatic flattening
options.C: Complete absence of any pulmonary vessels
options.D: No change to the appearance of the diaphragm

questions.explanation: In emphysema, overinflation of the lungs flattens the diaphragmatic dome, which results in an apparently small heart and a decreased cardiothoracic ratio on the chest radiograph — along with 'pruning' of the pulmonary vessels and, on lateral film, a large retrosternal translucency.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Thoracic Imaging — Chronic Airflow Limitation, Emphysema
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: The KT-1000 arthrometer is primarily used to measure which type of knee displacement?

options.A: Anteroposterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur
options.B: Medial-lateral joint space width only
options.D: Patellar height (Insall-Salvati ratio)

questions.explanation: The KT-1000 arthrometer is the most commonly used ligament testing device for the knee, measuring anteroposterior (forward-backward) displacement of the tibia relative to the femur, used to quantify ligamentous laxity (e.g. in ACL/PCL injury) as an adjunct to clinical assessment.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Ligament Testing Devices
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In the psychodynamic theory of OCD, the defense mechanism of 'undoing' is specifically responsible for the formation of:

options.A: Obsessions
options.B: Compulsions, which prevent or undo the feared consequences of the obsession
options.D: Obsessive-compulsive personality traits only, never actual symptoms

questions.explanation: According to the psychodynamic theory, 'isolation of affect' contributes to the formation of obsessions themselves, while 'undoing' is the defense mechanism that produces compulsions — behaviours aimed at preventing or undoing the feared consequences the obsession represents. Displacement, by contrast, is linked to phobic symptom formation.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Aetiology, Psychodynamic Theory
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Sharrard's postmortem motor neuron counts in poliomyelitis patients, cited in Daniels and Worthingham, found that by the time a muscle's MMT grade had fallen to 4 (Good), approximately what proportion of its motor neurons were already lost?

options.A: Less than 10%
options.B: About 25%
options.D: Nearly 100%

questions.explanation: Sharrard's data showed that more than half of a muscle's motor neurons were already gone by the time its MMT grade dropped to 4, which is why the text emphasizes that a 'Good' muscle already represents real, clinically significant weakness.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Glucocorticoid receptors are unique among the major receptor families in that they:

options.A: Are located on the cell surface and open ion channels directly
options.B: Are intracellular soluble proteins that, once liganded, dimerize and bind DNA to regulate gene transcription
options.D: Have no known endogenous ligand (are 'orphan receptors')

questions.explanation: Glucocorticoid receptors sit in the cytoplasm bound to HSP-90 and other inhibitory proteins. When the lipid-soluble steroid penetrates the cell and binds the receptor, HSP-90 is released, the receptor dimerizes, and the complex moves to the nucleus to bind glucocorticoid-responsive elements (GREs) on DNA, altering gene transcription — a fundamentally different, much slower mechanism than membrane receptors.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Following bilateral removal of the hippocampus and amygdala (to control severe epilepsy), the famous patient H.M. could still learn new motor/perceptual skills (like tracing a mirror-image star) without any conscious memory of having practiced them before. This dissociation illustrates the difference between:

options.A: Short-term memory and sensory memory
options.B: Procedural memory (how to do things) and declarative memory (memory of specific events)
options.D: Retrograde amnesia and anterograde amnesia only, with no other distinction

questions.explanation: H.M. retained procedural memory — he could learn and improve at tasks like mirror-tracing or the Tower of Hanoi over repeated sessions — even though he had no declarative (event) memory of ever having done the task before. This case was pivotal in showing procedural and declarative memory are at least partly separate systems.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Temporal-Lobe Association Cortex, Memory Functions
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: Lacunar strokes, caused by small penetrating-vessel disease deep in the cerebral white matter, are most strongly associated with which underlying conditions?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation and endocarditis only
options.B: Hypertensive small-vessel disease and diabetic microvascular disease
options.D: Berry aneurysm rupture

questions.explanation: Lacunar strokes result from small vessel (penetrating artery) disease deep in the cerebral white matter, and are strongly associated with chronic hypertension and diabetic microvascular disease, producing distinctive syndromes such as pure motor hemiplegia.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Lacunar Strokes
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter system is most strongly implicated in the GABA-benzodiazepine receptor theory of anxiety, given that drugs facilitating its transmission relieve anxiety while antagonists provoke it?

options.A: Dopamine
options.B: GABA (gamma-amino butyric acid)
options.D: Histamine

questions.explanation: GABA is the most prevalent inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS. Benzodiazepines facilitate GABA transmission and relieve anxiety, while benzodiazepine antagonists (e.g. flumazenil) and inverse agonists (e.g. beta-carbolines) provoke anxiety — strong evidence linking altered GABA function to the biological basis of anxiety disorders.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Neurotic, Stress-related and Somatoform Disorders — Anxiety Disorder, Aetiology
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: In a setting with a high local prevalence of C. difficile, why is alcohol gel decontamination between patient contacts considered inadequate?

options.A: Alcohol gel is more effective than hand-washing against C. difficile spores
options.B: Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores, so hands must be washed with soap and water instead
options.C: C. difficile cannot be transmitted via hands under any circumstances
options.D: Alcohol gel damages skin more than soap and water

questions.explanation: Alcohol gel decontamination is usually adequate for routine hand hygiene, but it does not kill C. difficile spores. In situations of high C. difficile prevalence (e.g. a local outbreak), hands must be washed with soap and water instead, since spores survive alcohol-based decontamination.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Infection Prevention and Control — Health Care-Associated Infection
questions.subject: Medicine

questions.question: Early strength gains observed in the first 2-3 weeks of a resistance training program are primarily attributed to:

options.A: Actual muscle fiber hypertrophy
options.B: Neural adaptation, since significant hypertrophy/vascularization changes typically require at least 6-12 weeks
options.C: An increase in the total number of muscle fibers (hyperplasia)
options.D: A change in bone density

questions.explanation: Strength gains in the first 2-3 weeks of resistance training are mainly the result of neural adaptation (improved motor unit recruitment and coordination), not muscle tissue change. Significant hypertrophy or increased vascularization typically requires at least 6-12 weeks of consistent training.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Duration
questions.subject: Kinesio Therapeutics
